items.title: OpenAI Countersues Apple, Alleging Stolen Secrets and Supplier Pressure
items.summary: On November 27, OpenAI filed counterclaims in California federal court accusing Apple of stealing trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices. The move follows Apple's July lawsuit against OpenAI and two former employees, which alleged misappropriation of Apple technology to support a consumer hardware push. OpenAI says Apple rehired a former employee who had access to confidential details about a new device and its hardware roadmap, and argues that Apple's employment practices trap staff and prevent them from working on competitors' technology. Apple denies the allegations and calls the counterclaims an attempt to distract from its own case. OpenAI says 400 employees have already moved from Apple to OpenAI.
items.impact: The dispute escalates a talent and intellectual-property battle over post-smartphone AI devices, where control of hardware and distribution may matter as much as model quality. The outcome could reshape how tech companies handle departing staff, personal devices and effective restrictions on working for rivals.

items.title: SAP Weighs Up to 10,000 Job Cuts as AI Reshapes Software Work
items.summary: SAP shares rose about 3% on November 27 after reports that the German software maker is preparing to cut as many as 10,000 roles while reshaping its business for the AI era. Reuters reported that all departments were asked to identify potential cuts, with engineering a particular focus. SAP employs more than 110,000 people and said the business environment is changing rapidly through AI, so it is continuously reviewing how its workforce needs to evolve. The company last cut roughly 10,000 jobs in 2024 through a voluntary departure programme. The reported plan follows four acquisitions this year aimed at organising company data, building AI models for business information and analysing workforce skills. Atlassian, Cloudflare and Microsoft have made similar AI-linked cuts.
items.impact: If confirmed, this would be one of the largest explicit AI-driven workforce reductions at a major enterprise software vendor, reinforcing a shift from headcount to AI productivity. It signals that efficiency gains, not just new products, are the near-term return investors expect from AI spending.

items.title: CISA Flags Exploited GeoServer and Drupal Flaws, Patches Due November 30
items.summary: CISA added three vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 27 based on evidence of active exploitation: CVE-2026-120705, an XML injection in OSGeo GeoServer; CVE-2026-129243, an incorrect-authorization flaw in GeoServer; and CVE-2026-136716, an improper check for unusual conditions in Drupal Core. Researchers say the two GeoServer bugs can be chained with other flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution, while the Drupal issue can let an unauthenticated attacker take over a site through its exposed installer when the installation is left in an affected incomplete state. Federal civilian agencies must remediate by November 30 under BOD 26-04, and CISA urges all organisations to prioritise these patches.
items.impact: Both products are widely deployed on public-facing government, university and enterprise websites, so exploitation could be broad and fast. The three-day federal deadline shows how the KEV catalog has become the de facto global patching queue for risk-based vulnerability management.

items.title: Booba Ransomware Jumps From a Water Plant Into Local-Government IT
items.summary: ThreatDown reported that Booba ransomware hit an unnamed water treatment plant on the U.S. East Coast during November and then reached the network of the local government overseeing it. The two environments were managed separately, and the plant side had no ThreatDown coverage. Responders isolated 48 machines on the government network - 40 workstations and eight servers - after encryption alerts; three were already encrypted and the other 45 were saved. The plant's computers were temporarily taken offline while a separate provider remediated them on site. ThreatDown said it found no evidence of water-service disruption, boil-water notices or manual operations, and no indicators of a nation-state actor. The account comes from the responder and has not been independently verified.
items.impact: The incident shows how a split IT/OT boundary can let an attack cross into a municipality's core network even when the utility itself keeps running. It is a near miss that argues for segmentation, shared logging and joint exercises between utilities and local government.

items.title: South Korea Activates Emergency Privacy Inspections as Breach Reports Double
items.summary: South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission said on November 27 it is activating an emergency response and inspection system after receiving 1,019 personal-data breach reports from January through October, about 2.3 times the 447 filed in all of 2025. Of those, 271 came from the public sector and 748 from the private sector. The regulator attributed much of the surge to AI-powered hacking that automates attacks and exploits neglected security debt: exposed internet-facing systems, stolen accounts and access keys, contractor servers, unused APIs and abandoned test servers. From December it will run three months of intensive inspections with ministries, local governments and high-risk private organisations, while sharing threat intelligence with the science ministry, financial regulator and intelligence service. Fines will fall for firms with adequate safeguards but stay strict for preventable breaches.
items.impact: The move turns AI-driven attack automation into a compliance and enforcement issue, with MFA, API inventories and vendor access becoming inspection priorities. It also marks a shift from post-incident punishment toward pre-emptive prevention and cross-agency intelligence sharing.
